title: Special glove helps people with paralyzed hands grasp objects: Study
source_used: Medical Dialogues (reporting a Technical University of Munich study in Nature Machine Intelligence)
key_facts: The Technical University of Munich (TUM) developed a soft, pneumatic glove (a 'soft-hand exoskeleton') that helps people with paralyzed hands grasp objects; the study is in Nature Machine Intelligence (2026).
A fabric glove carries air cushions inflated through 13 tubes; they bend and straighten each finger individually and rotate the wrist, to hold a plate, glass, fork or spoon.
Sensors on the forearm pick up the muscle's electrical signals, and machine learning predicts the intention to grasp; motion sensors keep the grip closed while the object is carried.
Researcher John Nassour says intentions are inferred from the signals with 97% reliability; the glove was sewn by hand from cheap fabric.

It was developed in close collaboration with a patient with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) who had little control of his hands but could still move the first thumb joint; the system recognized his intention in 9 of 10 cases.
He was able to reach for objects, hold a fork for the first time in four years, and pick up small cubes and drop them into a container; five minutes of video-game practice greatly improved his grasp.

The team is adapting the concept for other patients, such as stroke survivors; a neurologist says it could in principle help people with flaccid paralysis, such as after peripheral nerve damage or polyneuropathy.
quote_evidence: Despite very weak signals, the system recognized the patient’s intention in 9 out of 10 cases.

why_it_matters_hint: A cheap, soft assistive glove restored grasping in one man with severe ALS, but the evidence so far comes from one patient.
